summary: Defines URL schemes named tel, fax and modem for pointing at a terminal in the telephone network and the kind of connection to use. It is a standards-track document and was replaced by RFC 3966.

eli5.summary: A web link normally opens a page. This makes links that point to a phone number instead, so clicking one can start a call or a fax.

questions: how to write a phone number as a uri
subtitle: URL schemes for making phone calls and sending faxes from web links.

tldr.problem: Web pages and emails need a way to link to phone numbers, fax machines and data devices, just as they link to web pages and email addresses.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2806 defines three URL schemes: tel: for voice calls, fax: for facsimiles, and modem: for data connections. Each includes the phone number and optional parameters like subaddresses and post-dial sequences.
tldr.outcome: Users can click a tel: URL in a web page or email to initiate a call. The RFC was replaced by RFC 3966, which updated the syntax.

today: RFC 2806 was obsoleted by RFC 3966, which refined the syntax and updated the definitions for tel: and fax: URLs. The basic concept of phone number URLs remains in use, most commonly in the tel: scheme for initiating calls from web pages and email clients.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
RFC 2806 defines three new URL schemes for connecting to telecommunications devices: tel, fax, and modem. The tel: URL scheme is used for voice calls, answering machines and voice messaging systems. The fax: URL scheme connects to facsimile terminals. The modem: URL scheme initiates data calls on the public switched telephone network (POTS) or digital networks. The schemes are designed to work with international and local phone numbers, and include parameters for additional features like subaddresses and post-dial sequences.

These URLs use phone number notation based on the E.164 international standard and are compatible with hierarchical URLs like those for HTTP. The design emphasizes simplicity and human readability, making URLs suitable for printing, business cards and web pages.
sections.eli5: The URL schemes let you click a phone number on a web page or in an email to call someone or send a fax. The URL includes the phone number and information about what kind of call it is.

sections.title: URL Syntax and Structure
sections.content:
Each URL starts with a scheme name (tel, fax, or modem), followed by a colon and the subscriber information. A tel: URL has the form tel:+1-555-1234567 for a global number or tel:456-7890;phone-context=213 for a local number. The global form uses the E.164 international notation, which begins with a plus sign (+) followed by the country code and national number. Local numbers must include a phone-context parameter that qualifies them within a specific numbering area.

Additional parameters are separated by semicolons. ISDN subaddresses use ;isub= and T.33 fax subaddresses use ;tsub=. The post-dial parameter (;postd=) contains DTMF tones to send after the call connects, used for selecting extensions or invoking services. The ;tsp= parameter identifies a telephony service provider by domain name.
sections.eli5: A tel: URL starts with the scheme name, then the phone number, then extra parameters separated by semicolons. The phone number is written in international form with a plus sign, or in local form with a context that explains what area it is for.

sections.title: Three Call Types
sections.content:
The RFC defines three distinct URL schemes to specify the type of call desired. The tel: scheme indicates a voice call to a normal telephone, voice mailbox or service controlled by DTMF tones. The fax: scheme specifies a facsimile connection and may include T.33 fax subaddressing. The modem: scheme is for data calls and includes information about data capabilities. Modem URLs can specify required and recommended modem standards (such as V.32bis or V.90) along with serial port settings: the number of data bits (7 or 8), parity (none, even, odd, mark or space) and stop bits (1 or 2).

The distinction is necessary because digital telephone networks differentiate between these connection types and may route them to different equipment. For example, a call to the same phone number must specify tel: for voice or fax: for a facsimile machine to reach the correct device.
sections.eli5: The three schemes tell the phone system what kind of call it is: tel: for voice, fax: for faxes, and modem: for data. This matters because the phone network might route each type differently.

sections.title: Phone Numbers: Global and Local
sections.content:
Global phone numbers begin with a plus sign and follow E.164 notation, consisting of a country code (1 to 3 digits) and a national number. These numbers are unambiguous everywhere in the world and are always preferred when possible. Examples are +358-555-1234567 (Finland) and +1-555-1234567 (North America).

Local phone numbers omit the plus sign and are only meaningful within a specific numbering area. They must always include a phone-context parameter to indicate which area they apply to. The context can be a global-network-prefix (like +358 for Finland), a local-network-prefix (such as an area code), or a private-prefix (a named private network like a company PBX). Visual separators (hyphens, dots, parentheses) may be included in numbers for readability but are ignored during dialing.
sections.eli5: Global numbers start with a plus sign and work everywhere. Local numbers don't start with plus and only work in one area. Every local number must say which area it is for.

sections.title: Advanced Features
sections.content:
Post-dial sequences allow the URL to send DTMF tones after the call is established, useful for accessing voicemail systems, automated services or phone extensions. A URL like tel:+358-555-1234567;postd=pp22 tells the client to pause briefly (p), then send DTMF tones 2 and 2. The 'w' character waits for a dial tone, supporting complex dialing patterns used in some countries.

Subaddresses provide additional routing information. ISDN subaddresses use ;isub= and T.33 fax subaddresses use ;tsub= to direct the call to a specific endpoint within the same telephone number. Clients that do not support these features should ignore them and notify the user. Implementations are free to permit users to skip calls that require unsupported features.
sections.eli5: Post-dial sequences send button presses after the call connects, for selecting extensions or voicemail options. Subaddresses are extra numbers that route the call to a specific device when multiple devices share the same phone number.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A major concern with tel: URLs is that clicking them initiates expensive calls. The local entity MUST NOT place calls without the user's knowledge or consent, because of risks including call costs, wrong numbers inserted by malicious users, disruption of the user's phone line, opening data calls to potentially hostile hosts and revealing the user's phone number to the remote party.

Implementations SHOULD provide filtering so users can reject unwanted numbers, and MUST detect if a number is unavailable or if the call terminates unexpectedly, avoiding repeated dialing attempts. If the URL contains post-dial sequences but the client cannot send DTMF or pauses, the user SHOULD be notified and given the option to abort the call.
sections.eli5: Phone URLs can be dangerous because they cost money and might call the wrong number. Programs that handle tel: URLs must always ask permission first and let you review the number before dialing it.

fields.desc: A global number (starting with +) or local number (without +).
